blocks.title: This router cannot be automated yet
What to do
lines: PPPoE dialing and WAN Binding both write to the router, so neither is offered until the router answers for everything they depend on.
The OpenWRT Module settings page lists every check with what it costs. Once this blocking problem is cleared it also offers to install the missing packages it knows how to install.

blocks.title: Waiting for the router
lines: The two automations appear here as soon as the router answers over SSH. Nothing is wrong yet - the readiness checks have simply not run.

blocks.title: The automations are held back until the probe answers
lines: The machine is connected and the readiness probe is running. Nothing has been read off the router yet, so the pools and the binding instances further down this page would be drawn against no sample at all - and all three creates would refuse anyway, because none of them can tell what this router supports: Create a pool under PPPoE Dialer, and Bind one address to one WAN port and Create a WAN Binding instance under WAN Binding.
The probe repeats about every thirty seconds while this page is open. Check now asks immediately; if it never gets past this, Module settings names what the router is failing to answer.

blocks.title: Compatibility mode: no Bored Manager agent on this router
lines: Everything on this page is real and everything below still works. The module is driving the router over SSH, the way it always has.

What is missing is the safety net. A change that takes the connection down cannot undo itself, because there is nobody left on this side to tell it to; DHCP leases are read on a timer rather than as they happen; and a large PPPoE pool is written one round trip at a time.
Module settings, under Router packages, installs it - from a file on this machine when the router has no internet of its own.

blocks.title: Part of this page may refuse to run
lines: Something optional is missing. This page carries three creates - a pool, a binding instance and a one-to-one binding - and whichever of them the missing piece holds back will refuse with a specific reason and offer the install form for it on its own tab. OpenWRT Module settings names it and installs it too.

blocks.title: Nothing on this page is being acted on
lines: WAN Binding reconciles on the fast probe, and the fast probe has stopped producing samples. No device is being assigned, no lease change is noticed, and no failed WAN is remapped until it recovers. The session and assignment tables further down this page are the last good reading.
Reason below is what the last attempt returned. Refresh now, on any of the tabs that carry it, retries immediately; if it keeps failing, check that the machine entry is still connected over SSH.

blocks.title: Session and WAN state below may be out of date
lines: The rest of the fast probe is answering, but the interface dump came back unreadable and the module is keeping the last list it could parse. Every PPPoE session state, every WAN state and the free-WAN counts each binding instance reports are read from that old list.
A session that has since dialled still reads as dialing, and a WAN that has since failed still reads as available - so binding can hand a client a WAN that is already down.

The usual cause is a pool large enough that the dump no longer fits in one answer. Raising the fast interval, in Settings, General, Update intervals, or shrinking the managed pool is what clears it; the module retries on its own every few ticks.

rows.label: Age of the last fast sample

blocks.title: How pools behave
lines: A pool is one carrier and a list of VLANs; each VLAN dials its own PPPoE session with its own routing table and, in shared-account mode, its own derived MAC. The router owns all of it: bm-pppoe-pool derives the interfaces, the tagged devices and the firewall zone from the pool record and reconciles them on every change.

Every member always has a row. Unwritten means the record names a member whose interface section is missing on the router - a create that stopped part way, or a section removed by hand. Applying any edit to the pool writes exactly the difference and repairs it.
Disable stops a session and keeps it stopped across reboots; Stop is the one-off. The router's own watchdog redials sessions that stay down - its timing is under Daemon settings.
Editing a pool applies to every interface in it in one pass. The check runs on the router and its findings are the same sentences LuCI and bmpppoe show.

blocks.title: The router stopped answering
lines: Everything below is the last answer the pool daemon gave. Nothing has been forgotten - the pools live on the router - but nothing here is live until it answers again. Refresh now retries immediately.

blocks.title: Derived, read-only
lines: Interface names derive from the prefix and the VLAN: prefix fpt, VLAN 101 is section fpt101 on kernel device pppoe-fpt101, dialling over carrier.101. Its routing table and metric are table base + VLAN.

With MAC mode auto, each tagged member is assigned 02:xx:xx:xx:VV:VV - hashed from the carrier MAC and the pool id, with the VLAN in the last two octets - stable across reboots and reconciles. The untagged member (VLAN 0) always keeps the carrier's own MAC.
The id, the mode and the prefix cannot change: every derived name embeds them. Delete the pool and create a new one to change them.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Label - Only for people; shown wherever the pool is.
Service name / Access concentrator / AC MAC address - PPPoE discovery filters. Empty means autodetect, which is right for almost every ISP.

Username and Password - The shared account. Only used by shared-account pools; per-VLAN pools carry accounts on the Members tab. An empty password keeps the stored one; changing it redials every session.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Members - The pool's whole member list; applying replaces it. A VLAN missing from the list is removed - its session taken down and its interface deleted - and a new one is added with its firewall membership in the same pass.
Shared-account pools list VLANs: ranges and numbers, like 101-150,200,0. VLAN 0 means untagged on the bare carrier, at most once per pool.

Per-VLAN pools list one member per line: VLAN, username, password - separated by a comma, tab, semicolon, pipe or spaces. A kept VLAN may leave the username or password empty to keep what is stored; a new VLAN needs all three. Lines starting with # are ignored.

blocks.title: High-risk fields
lines: Everything below redials the pool or moves what it owns. Changing the carrier redials every session on the new uplink. Changing the table base moves every routing table - binding rules pointing at the old ones go stray until bm-wanbind's next pass. Changing the MAC mode presents changed MACs to the BRAS. Extra pppd options are passed verbatim: a wrong word fails every session.
The check names the exact impact before anything is written.

options.label: auto - one derived MAC per VLAN
inherit - every VLAN keeps the carrier MAC

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: MTU - Empty uses the pppd default of 1492. Above 1492 needs an ISP that supports RFC 4638.
LCP echo failures / interval - Presume the peer dead after this many missed echoes sent this many seconds apart. Empty leaves pppd's default of 5 and 1.
IPv6 - Disabled is the pool default; Automatic negotiates when the ISP offers it.
Use ISP DNS servers - Off means the DNS servers field is written per member instead; it is ignored while this is on.
Default route - Each session installs its default route into its own routing table, which is what a binding rule points a client at.

Host-Uniq - Raw hex bytes; leave empty unless the ISP requires it. Inactivity timeout - seconds of idle before hangup, 0 keeps sessions up. PADI attempts and timeout - discovery retries; empty leaves pppd's defaults.

Carrier - The physical uplink every member dials over. MAC mode - auto derives 02:... per VLAN from the carrier MAC, the pool id and the VLAN, stable across reboots; shared-account pools require it. Table base - each member routes in base + VLAN. Extra pppd options - passed to pppd verbatim, for the options this form does not carry.

fields.label: Allow LAN to reach this zone

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Zone - 1-11 letters, digits or underscores. The pool's members sit in it by explicit membership, written and reconciled by the router's pool daemon; pools may share one zone, and changing it moves every membership - the old zone is removed when nothing else uses it.
Masquerade and MTU fix - What a WAN zone needs: SNAT and MSS clamping. On a shared zone the union of what its pools ask wins.
Allow LAN to reach this zone - Writes one forwarding from the LAN zone, so clients can actually use the sessions.

blocks.title: What deleting removes
lines: Every interface in the pool is taken down and its section removed, with its tagged VLAN device and derived MAC. Every routing table the members used stops being written. The pool's zone memberships are removed, and the zone itself goes when no other pool uses it and WAN Binding is not installed. The record is removed last, so an interrupted delete can simply be run again.

The router refuses while a bm-wanbind instance hands clients to this carrier, and this page refuses while a binding instance is running on it - stop the instance first, with Stop on its row under WAN Binding, Instances.
The accounts themselves are not touched; they live wherever the list came from.

actions.label: Delete this pool
actions.confirm: Delete the whole pool - every interface, VLAN device, routing table and firewall membership it owns? Anybody dialling through it loses their connection.

fields.label: macvlan (kmod-macvlan) - per-slot MACs in Direct mode

blocks.title: The pool daemon comes from Router packages
lines: Pools are owned by bm-pppoe-pool 2.x on the router. If the check below says the pool daemon is missing or too old, install or update the router packages from Module settings, Router packages - the form unlocks when the router answers with it.

blocks.title: Tagged, untagged, and shared accounts
lines: Carrier mode VLAN tags each member as 802.1Q. Direct dials the carrier itself, untagged - the flow for an ISP that answers PPPoE without 802.1Q. Direct has no VLAN 0; slots are 1-4094.

MAC mode auto derives one MAC per member (a tagged device in VLAN mode, a macvlan in Direct - needs kmod-macvlan). inherit keeps the carrier MAC; Direct then derives a Host-Uniq per slot so sessions on one wire can be told apart.
A shared account carries as many sessions as the ISP allows. Try two or three members before pasting the full list.
One account per VLAN is the safe mode: each line has its own login.
Nothing is written until the check passes and you apply. The check runs on the router itself and names every derived interface, table and MAC decision it would make.

options.label: Direct - dial the carrier itself, untagged
auto - one derived MAC per member
inherit - every member keeps the carrier MAC

fields.label: Allow LAN to reach this zone

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Mode - Fixed for the life of the pool; delete and recreate to change it.
Pool id - 1-31 lowercase letters, digits or underscores. This is what you delete it by. Label - only for people.

Carrier - The physical uplink; the router lists what qualifies. Carrier mode - VLAN tags each member; Direct dials the carrier untagged. MAC mode - auto derives one MAC per member; inherit keeps the carrier MAC. Prefix - 1-4 characters, fixed after create; interface names derive from it: prefix fpt, member 101 dials as fpt101 on pppoe-fpt101.
VLANs / slots - Ranges and numbers, like 101-150,200. In VLAN mode, 0 means untagged, at most once. In Direct mode slots are 1-4094. Username and Password - the one account every member dials with.
Table base - Each member routes in table base + VLAN; the pool records its own base on the router.
Service name, Access concentrator, AC MAC - PPPoE discovery filters; empty means autodetect.

MTU - Empty uses the pppd default of 1492; above 1492 needs RFC 4638. LCP echo failures/interval - dead-peer detection; empty leaves pppd's defaults. IPv6, ISP DNS, DNS servers, Default route, Host-Uniq, Inactivity timeout, PADI attempts/timeout, Extra pppd options - the same options LuCI's PPPoE form carries, applied to every member.
Firewall zone - Created and owned by the router's pool daemon; pools may share one. Masquerade and MTU fix shape it; Allow LAN writes one forwarding from the LAN zone.

options.label: Direct - dial the carrier itself, untagged
inherit - every member keeps the carrier MAC
auto - one derived MAC per member

fields.label: Allow LAN to reach this zone

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Mode - Fixed for the life of the pool. Pool id, Label, Carrier, Carrier mode, Prefix - as on the shared-account tab; the prefix is fixed after create.
MAC mode - inherit keeps the carrier's MAC on every member; auto derives a stable per-member MAC (802.1Q device in VLAN mode, macvlan in Direct).

Member list file / Members - One member per line: VLAN or slot, username, password - separated by a comma, tab, semicolon, pipe or spaces; # starts a comment. The file wins over the pasted text. In Direct mode the first column is a slot 1-4094, not a VLAN tag.
Everything below the member list is the same set of options as the shared-account tab, applied to every member.

blocks.title: The router's own watchdog
lines: netifd retries a failing PPPoE session by itself, and it is better at it than anything polling from outside. The watchdog on the router is for the sessions netifd has given up on: anything down longer than the redial delay is taken down and dialled again, longest-down first, at most one batch per pass.
These numbers live on the router, in /etc/config/bm_pppoe, and apply immediately: the counter timer is re-armed and the next watchdog pass uses them.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Counter interval - 1 to 300 seconds. How often the router reads /proc/net/dev and corrects its session table.
Redial after - 0 to 86400 seconds. How long a session may stay down before the watchdog redials it; 0 turns the watchdog off and leaves every retry to netifd.
Redial batch - 1 to 500. The most redials one watchdog pass starts: a provider that has just dropped four hundred sessions does not want four hundred simultaneous reconnects from one router.

blocks.title: This router does not answer for WAN Binding
lines: Every instance, every one-to-one binding, the routing tables behind them and every ip rule they use are kept by bm-wanbind on the router itself. This module asks it and sends changes to it; it writes none of that. Without the router packages there is nothing to ask, so the tables on these tabs are empty because nothing was read - not because this router is carrying nothing.
The sentence below is the readiness check’s own. Router packages, under Module settings, is where the packages are installed, and Check again re-reads the router once they are.

An instance or a one-to-one binding this module created before the router kept its own is handed to the daemon by itself once it is there, with the priority and the table it was stamped with, so the rules already standing are adopted rather than written a second time. Nothing here has to be pressed for that.

blocks.title: Something about WAN Binding needs saying
lines: The sentence below is not a call that failed - this router is answering. It is the router disagreeing with something it was asked for, or a record this module still holds that the daemon has not taken over yet, and it is the only place either is stated.

Where it names something made before the router kept its own binding, that thing is offered to the daemon again on every pass, with the priority and the table it was stamped with. Its ip rules stand exactly where they were meanwhile, and traffic still follows them - what has stopped is anything reacting to a change. Fix what the sentence names and the next pass finishes the handover; nothing here has to be pressed.

blocks.title: What these numbers count
lines: The tiles and the donut add up every binding instance's WAN pool at once. A router with four instances has four separate pools, and the question worth asking about all of them together is how many ports are left to hand out.

Available is a healthy WAN nobody holds and Bound is one a device is using, so those two together are the pool. Warning is a WAN that came back so recently the module does not trust it yet, Error is one that failed, and Dialing is a PPPoE session still negotiating - none of the three can be handed to a device, which is why a full pool with a large Error count still leaves people waiting.

The one-to-one tiles count hand-placed bindings instead of pool ports. Held is the one to watch, and it counts every binding whose rule points at the unreachable table: the ones whose WAN is down, and the ones whose device has walked off the LAN it was bound on while its owner had chosen Keep it off the internet. Either way that address has no way out at all until the WAN comes back or the device comes home.
The charts read this module's own history and follow the range picker above the page, so they keep filling in for as long as the module is running rather than only while this tab is open.

blocks.title: Why this is offered here
lines: This router is missing a package binding depends on. The form below this one checks before it writes, so a create here would refuse and name it - and naming it, then sending you to another page, is a longer way round than doing it.

It is the same flow as Module settings: the check reads free space and whether the router has a route to the internet and changes nothing, and only names from this module's own fixed list ever reach a command line.
Applying runs a job and then re-reads the router. What that re-read finds is what unlocks the form.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Policy routing (ip-full) - The one thing a create on this tab is actually gated on, since a one-to-one binding is a policy rule and nothing else. Some targets ship the BusyBox applet, which has no ip rule subcommand at all.

DHCP leases (dnsmasq) - Not what this form needs. A binding on a typed address does not ask for it at all: nothing has to be leasing for a rule on a typed address to work. It is ticked because this section is raised for binding as a whole, and the instance half - Create an instance, two tabs along - does require it. It is also where a binding that names a MAC finds its address, so on a router without it such a binding is created and then waits for a lease nothing will ever read.
PPPoE support (ppp, ppp-mod-pppoe, kmod-pppoe) - What the pool form under PPPoE Dialer needs; nothing on this tab uses it. A group already present is skipped.

blocks.title: What a one-to-one binding does to the router
lines: A one-to-one binding is a single policy rule: traffic from this one address looks up the routing table belonging to the WAN port named here, before the router's main table is consulted at all. The rule is written at its own priority, below every priority a binding instance writes in, so where the two would both apply this one is read first and the address leaves through the port chosen here whatever the instance would have handed it.
Nothing else about the device changes. It keeps its DHCP lease, its LAN and its firewall zone; what is added is that one rule and the firewall forwarding that lets that LAN reach that WAN.

Keep it off the internet is what happens by default when the WAN goes down: the rule is re-pointed at the module's unreachable table, so the address has no way out and whoever is using it sees a dead connection rather than a different one. This is deliberate, and it is not what a rule left pointing at an empty table would do - the kernel does not fail that lookup, it falls through to the next rule and then to the main table, and the device quietly leaves by the router's default connection. That silent exit is the whole reason this setting exists.

Let it use the default connection is the opposite trade, and it is still a rule rather than the absence of one. While the WAN is down the rule stays at this binding's own priority and is re-pointed at the main table, so the address leaves by the router's ordinary default connection; it goes back to the WAN's own table the moment that WAN is usable again. On a LAN a binding instance owns, taking the rule off the router instead would be a total outage: that instance's fail-closed catch-all matches the address the instant the one-to-one rule is gone, so the option chosen to keep a device online would have taken it off the network entirely. A rule naming the main table reaches the default connection from underneath that catch-all, and reads the same on a router carrying no instance at all. Choose it when being reachable at all matters more than which port the traffic left by.

blocks.title: Bind one address to one WAN port

options.label: Let it use the default connection

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Binding name - A label for people, unique among the one-to-one bindings on this router. It reaches job labels and the event trail, so it is one line of ordinary text.

What this binding names - An IP address binds whatever holds that address. A device MAC follows the device instead: the rule is rewritten when its DHCP lease moves to another address, and it is kept for the lease release grace once the lease disappears before it is withdrawn.

Address or MAC - The address itself, or twelve hexadecimal digits in colon form. An IP has to sit inside a subnet carried by an interface this router describes as one of its own LANs rather than as an uplink, because that interface's firewall zone is what the forwarding is written from - so an address can be inside a subnet the router really carries and still be refused, if the interface carrying it reads as the way this router reaches the internet.

That reading is never taken from what an interface is called. It is weighed from what the configuration states about it: the dnsmasq sections in /etc/config/dhcp, whether its firewall zone masquerades on a router where another zone does, the IPv6 prefix it delegates, whether it names a gateway, whether its address is one the public internet routes to, and the protocol netifd reports. Where those statements do not settle it the interface is called unclear and is still searched, so a LAN the router says nothing useful about does not disappear. A refusal names the interface, the subnets it looked in and the evidence it read, which is how a misclassified LAN can be told apart from a mistyped octet.

A MAC with no current DHCP lease has no address to place, so it can only be bound on a router with exactly one candidate LAN - counting the interfaces whose role the configuration does not settle. On a router with two or more, connect the device once and check again: choosing between them would be a guess written into a firewall forwarding.

WAN port - The uplink this address leaves through. The list is built from the last router sample, so a port added since this tab was opened is not in it - press Refresh now above and check the form again, which is what the refusals that name a WAN this module has not seen are asking for. A PPPoE pool cannot crowd the rest of the router out of this list: the sessions fill what is left after every other interface has a place. Nothing else is hidden from it either, so one of this router's own LANs can appear here - Check this binding is what refuses that pick, and it names the interface and the evidence rather than leaving the row out.

When that WAN is down - The note above describes both choices. The default keeps the address off the internet rather than letting it out by a route nobody chose; it can be changed later from the row without touching anything else.

blocks.title: The last pass did not finish
lines: The rows below are the last ones the module was able to compute, and the router has been free to change since. A binding shown as bound may already have lost its rule.

blocks.title: Something about these bindings needs saying
lines: The sentence below is about where the bindings live and whether this app can currently reach them - not about a pass that failed. A binding the router holds keeps working while it is showing.

blocks.title: Not every row here was placed by hand
lines: The router reports both halves of binding through one call, so this table carries the seats binding instances are holding as well as the bindings somebody wrote. Source tells them apart: manual is a section written here or at a router shell, and anything else is the id of the instance holding that seat.

Only a manual row can be renamed, switched off or deleted. Editing a seat here would be this page reaching into the other half’s work, and the instance would take it straight back on its next pass - a change that appeared to succeed, showed for a few seconds and then undid itself with nothing anywhere to explain it. The row actions refuse it and name the instance instead.
To free a seat, use Unassign or Reassign on that instance’s own Assignments table, under Instances.

blocks.title: The target, the WAN, the priority and the table are fixed
lines: All four were stamped when this binding was created, and the rule sitting on the router right now was written from those exact numbers. Changing one here would leave that rule where it is - owned by nobody, still steering that address - while the module went looking for its own rule at a priority nothing was ever written to. Delete this binding and create the one you want instead.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Binding name - A label for people; it has to stay unique among the one-to-one bindings on this router.

When that WAN is down - Keep it off the internet re-points the rule at the unreachable table so the address has no way out; Let it use the default connection re-points it at the main table instead, which reaches the router's default connection from underneath any instance catch-all. Neither one removes the rule: it stays at the Rule priority shown under What was stamped, and what is on the router below, and Rule as it should stand there names the table it is looking up, so it can be compared with ip -4 rule show by eye. The change is applied on the next pass.

Enabled - Switching it off takes the rule off the router and stops reserving the address, so a binding instance serving that LAN is free to hand the device a WAN of its own again. The binding itself stays on the router, switched off, so switching it back on writes the same rule at the same priority: the router kept the number. Switching it back on is the same action as the row's Enable button and is refused on the same terms, in the same words - a router with no firewall to write a forwarding into cannot carry a binding, and neither door will pretend otherwise. Only the switch is held to that. A rename, and a change to When that WAN is down, go through on a router that can do nothing else at all, because they are the edits this form exists to allow when something is already wrong; and switching one off is never refused, whatever the router has lost. A refused Save writes nothing, so the binding is left exactly as the router holds it - untick Enabled and Save again to keep the rest. Every field a Save does send is read back off the router first, so a change somebody else made while this form was open is not undone by a field you did not touch.

blocks.title: One LAN client, one WAN
lines: An instance owns exactly one logical LAN and one physical WAN carrier. Interfaces outside that pair remain independent.
A sticky client keeps its WAN by MAC address. Optional remapping moves it only after the WAN has stayed failed beyond the grace period.
A newly leased device is assigned a random free WAN; when none is free it waits in FIFO order. New instances are created on the Create an instance tab, the next one along.

Per WAN is how many devices may share one line: one client per WAN is a line each, a number is that many sharing, no limit puts every device this instance sees on the pool however small it is. It is stamped at creation and cannot be changed.

Why is the daemon’s own sentence about a section it will not accept. Such an instance installs no rule, seats nobody and appears in none of the tables below, so its row would otherwise be nothing but zeroes with nothing anywhere saying what is wrong with it.

blocks.title: Operational warning
lines: A waiting device deliberately has no internet: a catch-all unreachable route stops it leaking through the router's default WAN.
Pausing the fast OpenWRT interval pauses this automation.

blocks.title: Above roughly 1,000 clients, three limits are yours to raise

lines: At that size the check reports conntrack, neighbour-table and flow-offload findings. They are router-wide values that affect every service on the box, so they are applied from one deliberate place rather than silently during a create: Module settings, Router limits, which reads them live, sizes a recommendation to this router, applies through the router's own agent or over SSH, and persists them under /etc/sysctl.d/ so they survive a reboot.

The dnsmasq lease limits the same check reports are not router-wide, so they are handled by the create itself - the checkbox called Raise dnsmasq lease limits when needed, on the form under Create an instance, raises them for you.
The shell below runs on the router itself, for anything beyond what those two cover.

blocks.title: The LAN, the carrier, the address range and Per WAN are fixed
lines: Every client rule and the safety catch-all were installed for this exact LAN, carrier and address range, so changing any of the three would leave rules on the router pointing at addresses that are no longer behind this instance. Delete the instance and create one for the scope you want instead.

Addresses served is the window this instance may hand a WAN to - the whole LAN, or the range it was created with. A device whose lease falls outside that window never enters this instance's pass, so it appears in none of the tables below and is not waiting for anything.

Per WAN is fixed for a harder reason than the other three: the rule priorities this instance holds were reserved for the number it was created with, so there is no room to seat more devices than that number allowed. Delete it and create one with the number you want.

lines: Instance name - A display label only. It must be unique on this router.
Keep a device on the same WAN - Remember the WAN by client MAC and prefer it after a lease IP change or a reconnect. Switching it off drops the choices already remembered for this instance.
Remap after a WAN failure - When a WAN stays in error longer than the configured grace period, move its client to another free WAN. Both flags take effect on the next reconcile.

Only the devices whose WAN is not healthy right now - failing, dialing, still inside its warning window, or gone from the pool altogether. This tab is open by default because the other one re-reads every assignment on each update, and only the tab you are looking at is fetched.

blocks.title: Why this is offered here
lines: This router is missing a package this automation depends on. The form below checks before it writes, so a create here would refuse and name it - and naming it, then sending you to another page, is a longer way round than doing it.

It is the same flow as Module settings: the check reads free space and whether the router has a route to the internet and changes nothing, and only names from this module's own fixed list ever reach a command line.
Applying runs a job and then re-reads the router. What that re-read finds is what unlocks the form.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: PPPoE support (ppp, ppp-mod-pppoe, kmod-pppoe) - What the pool form under PPPoE Dialer needs; nothing on this tab uses it. A group already present is skipped.
Policy routing (ip-full) - What the WAN Binding form below needs. Some targets ship the BusyBox applet, which has no ip rule subcommand at all.
DHCP leases (dnsmasq) - Where WAN Binding finds the devices it assigns. Without it the device table stays empty.

blocks.title: Both forms check before they write
lines: Check reads the router and changes nothing. It reports what apply would do and refuses outright when the router cannot support it; only then does the apply button unlock.
A check result is single-use and expires after ten minutes, and it is tied to the exact values that were checked - editing a field means checking again.

Applying starts a job. It writes to the router in bounded chunks and can be cancelled between them - whatever was already written stays on the router, and the module keeps only the part that committed.

blocks.title: Two of the three lists are read once, when this tab opens
lines: DHCP LAN interface and WAN carrier are both built from the last router sample. Before the first sweep lands they are empty, and an interface added since this tab was opened is not in them. Which addresses on that LAN is not one of these: its two choices are fixed and always offered.
Press Refresh now at the top of this tab, then leave this tab and come back: the lists are rebuilt each time the tab becomes visible.

Each list holds at most 500 rows, and the count is not what hides a device from you. On WAN carrier the only rows that ever fall off it are the tail of a PPPoE pool past that number: every device the pool is not riding on is kept, and so is the carrier the pool rides on. DHCP LAN interface cannot be filled by a pool at all, since a session's own protocol keeps it out of that list. So a device missing from either list is a device the router had not reported when this tab opened, which is what Refresh now puts back - the one thing it cannot put back is a pool member past the five hundredth row.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Instance name - A unique display label for this one LAN and one carrier pair.

DHCP LAN interface - The logical OpenWRT interface whose IPv4 DHCP leases are assigned. It must have a subnet and a dnsmasq DHCP section; when dnsmasq itself is missing, Module settings can install it.

That list hides nothing. Every interface carrying an IPv4 address and running static or dhcp is in it, this router's own uplinks included, because a dropdown cannot read /etc/config to tell a LAN from a WAN - and hiding the interface somebody came here to use, with nothing on screen to say why, costs more than offering one they will not pick. Pick the interface the clients are on: an instance hands a WAN to every DHCP client it sees on the interface named here and writes its firewall forwardings from that interface's own zone, so one rooted on an uplink would be distributing the pool upstream of this router rather than behind it. Check the scope warns when /etc/config/dhcp switches the DHCP server off for the interface, which is what a stock uplink's own section does, and it refuses the pick outright when the router's own configuration - a next hop under option gateway, a firewall zone that masquerades, an address the public internet routes to, a protocol that dials or takes a lease - reads that interface as an uplink. The refusal names the interface and quotes the lines it read, and says what to change if it has read the router wrong. Where nothing in /etc/config settles which side of the router an interface is on it says nothing at all, so that pick is still yours to get right.

Which addresses on that LAN - Every DHCP client is the whole LAN, which is what every instance did before this option existed. Only an address range narrows it: leases inside the range are given a WAN of their own, and every other device on that LAN is left completely alone - it keeps using the router's normal connection, and no rule is written for it either way.

First address / Last address - Read only when the range is chosen, and both have to sit inside the subnet of the LAN chosen above. A rule this instance writes selects on a source address behind that LAN, so an address outside the subnet could never match one, and the check refuses rather than writing a rule nothing can hit. The range is turned into whole address blocks for the safety rule, so a wide range costs a handful of rules rather than one per address.

The choice of whole LAN or range cannot be changed afterwards, for the same reason the LAN and the carrier cannot: every client rule and the safety rule were installed for exactly this scope. Delete the instance and create it again to change it.
WAN carrier - A device, or one VLAN on a device when the ISP hands out the uplink tagged. Every PPPoE, DHCP, or static WAN using it, directly or through one of its VLANs, becomes part of the pool.

Clients per WAN - a whole number from 0 to 4096, default 1. 1 gives every device a WAN of its own, which is what every release before this one did: the pool runs out when there are more devices than WANs and the rest queue. A larger number lets that many devices share one WAN, so twenty lines at five seats a hundred devices before anybody waits. 0 is no limit, and on a pool of one WAN that reads as every device on this LAN leaving by that one line.

That number cannot be changed afterwards either. The rule priorities an instance holds were reserved for the number it was created with, so raising it later would need a band it was never given; delete the instance and create it again.
Keep a device on the same WAN - Remember the WAN by client MAC and prefer it after a lease IP change or a reconnect, when that WAN is free and healthy.
Remap after a WAN failure - When a WAN stays in error longer than the configured grace period, move its client to another free WAN.

Raise dnsmasq lease limits when needed - Allow apply to raise this LAN's DHCP limit and the global dnsmasq lease cap to the size the check reports. That restarts dnsmasq, which briefly interrupts DHCP and DNS for the whole router; leave it off and the check still reports the numbers to set by hand.

blocks.title: What this reads, and what it will never touch
lines: Every other table on this page shows what this module asked the router for. This one asks for the whole ip rule table on a timer - not only the priority bands WAN Binding writes in - so a rule somebody added by hand, one left behind by another package, or one from an older release of this module is visible here and nowhere else in the app.

Each row says which routing table the rule sends that address to, which WAN that table’s default route actually leaves through, and how that compares with the main table’s default. That is the whole question the page answers: whether an address is on the router’s normal connection or somewhere else, and who put it there. The verdict is the daemon’s own, because it holds the sections, the bands and the kernel’s dumps at once - a priority on its own cannot tell an instance’s client rule from a hand-written one at the same number.

Most of what a multi-WAN router carries here is the router routing itself. netifd writes three rules for every interface given a routing table of its own - its address to its table, traffic addressed to it to its table, and traffic the router sends out of it - so a box dialling thirty-two PPPoE sessions has ninety-six of them before anybody has bound anything. They are neither this module’s work nor a stranger’s, and counting them as either buries the handful of rows worth reading.

Nothing on this page ever changes a rule it did not write. A row marked as written outside this module is reported and left exactly where it is - quietly deleting somebody else's policy rule from a page they never opened is not a thing this module will do.

The scan runs while the Connection page is open - any tab of it, not only this one - at the interval under Module settings, Advanced rules, in the field called Binding scan interval. Scan now asks for one pass immediately.

The counts above describe what was read, not what is on the router. Anything this module writes sits at high priorities, so its own rules are the first to fall off the end: read an empty owner column as “not in this scan” rather than as “not on this router”.

blocks.title: The numbers an instance is stamped with
lines: Everything on this form is bm-wanbind’s own configuration on the router, in /etc/config/bm_wanbind. This module keeps no copy of any of it. Until 3.4.0 it kept one under Module settings, wrote ip rules from that copy while the daemon wrote its own from this one, and the two removed each other’s work every pass - thirty-four rules deleted every thirty seconds on a real router, with every surface green because each half was doing exactly what it had been told.

Only the pass interval acts on what is already running: the router re-arms its timer rather than waiting out the old one. Every other number here is the default an instance is stamped with when it is created afterwards. A section already on the router keeps the numbers it has, because those are what the ip rules standing in its kernel were written against, so moving a base here moves nothing that is already routing.
To renumber an instance that already exists, delete it and create it again.

blocks.title: How the daemon numbers and times its work
What each field means
lines: Pass interval - 5 to 3600 seconds, default 30. How often the daemon reconciles: it seats new leases, moves clients off failed WANs, and puts back any rule in the bands it owns that has gone missing.

New-WAN warning window - 0 to 3600 seconds, default 5. A WAN that has just come up is held in Warning this long and is not handed to a device, so a flapping uplink shows as flapping instead of being given out and taken back.
WAN error grace - 0 to 3600 seconds, default 20. A failed WAN has to stay failed this long before an instance set to remap moves its client somewhere else.
Lease release grace - 0 to 86400 seconds, default 120. How long a WAN stays reserved for a device after its DHCP lease disappears, so a machine that reboots comes back to the line it had.

Keep LAN traffic local - on by default. One rule per LAN, `to <that LAN> lookup main`, numbered from the LAN-local base and consulted before every binding rule, so a bound device still reaches the devices beside it. Off, a one-to-one rule sends every packet from that address out of its WAN - the ones for its own LAN included, which leave by the WAN port addressed to a private network that drops them.

LAN-local rule priority base - 1000 to 27999, default 18000. Sixty-four priorities from here, one per LAN. It has to end below the one-to-one base and below every instance's assignment base, because a rule read after a binding's own decides nothing.

One-to-one rule priority base - 1000 to 28000, default 19000. A binding placed by hand takes one priority from a band 1000 wide starting here, and that band has to end before the assignment base. A binding numbered inside the instance band is adopted by that instance as one of its own seats, found to have no lease behind it and deleted on the next pass - once every pass, for ever, with nothing anywhere saying why that address keeps losing its WAN.

Assignment rule priority base - 1000 to 28999, default 20000. Where an instance starts numbering its client rules. They run from here up to, but not including, the catch-all base, so that gap is also the most clients one instance could ever seat; at least 64 have to be left in it.

Catch-all rule priority base - 2000 to 29999, default 30000. Each instance takes one priority from here for its fail-closed rule, the one that stops a device it has not seated yet from leaking out through the router’s default connection.

Catch-all routing table - 2000 to 32766, default 253. The table holding an unreachable default. A waiting device and a held one-to-one binding are both pointed at it, which is why they have no way out rather than a different one. The router’s own main and local tables are refused by name: an unreachable default written into either takes the router off the network.
WAN routing table base - 1000 to 25000, default 10000. Where the daemon numbers the routing table it gives each WAN in a pool.

A value already in force is accepted whatever the window above says. Two of the daemon’s shipped defaults sit outside these windows - the catch-all base at 30000 and the catch-all table at 253 - so a form opened on a stock router would otherwise refuse to save a pass interval because of a number nobody had touched.

A blank field keeps the value in force, and only what actually changes is sent. The daemon’s own switch is not on this form and is never sent from it: turning it off takes every instance’s rules off the router, and a checkbox reports false when it is simply absent, so one saved pass interval would have taken every pool off the air.

blocks.title: Bounded background work
lines: A running job lives in memory and cannot resume after the app restarts. Reconciliation repairs whatever router state that leaves behind.
Cancel stops the steps that have not started; a command already running on the router is allowed to finish.
A step can also finish as a warning: the router took the change and then did not show it. The job carries on, and the warning is kept in the history.

blocks.title: What lands here
lines: Everything the automation decided on its own: a device bound or moved, a session created or deleted, a firewall rule that verified empty, a watchdog redial, a router reboot the module recovered from.

Binding events belong to one instance and also appear in that instance's own row detail under WAN Binding, Instances. PPPoE and router events belong to the router rather than to any instance, so this table is the only place in the app that shows them.
The list is bounded per router, so the oldest entries are dropped. Nothing here ever carries router command output, because a rejected uci line can contain a PPPoE password.
